extracted.intended_audience: researchers in experimental philosophy/psychology of mathematics, mathematical-aesthetics researchers, and mathematicians interested in empirical methods for measuring aesthetic judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and analysing empirical studies that measure agreement about mathematical beauty (equations or proofs) across cultures and expertise levels, using comparative judgement and related psychometric/statistical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardy’s six criteria for beauty in a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy’s list of six criteria for beauty in a proof: economy, significance, depth, generality, unexpectedness, and inevitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy treats economy (simplicity) as facilitating grasp in a single act of mental apprehension; identifying these criteria requires a high degree of technical proficiency developed through many years of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative judgement (CJ) as measurement method
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pairwise comparative judgements (which of two objects is more beautiful) rather than absolute rating scales to measure aesthetic judgements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: does not require pre-determined criteria and therefore suits ambiguous/fuzzy concepts; participants are better at relative judgements than absolute ones; CJ constructs a scaled rank order from collective pairwise judgements (Bisson et al. 2016). Successful precedents include measuring conceptual understanding, proof comprehension, and explanatoriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer relative (pairwise) judgments over absolute ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative judgements may reveal underlying consensus that absolute scales obscure because individuals have different absolute standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental evidence and theory from psychophysics suggest humans are more reliable at comparative judgements (Thurstone, Laming, Pollack). Comparative methods can circumvent reference-group effects and subjective scale-use differences across cultures/participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bradley–Terry model for scoring pairwise judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse pairwise CJ data with the Bradley–Terry model, which assigns each stimulus an estimated parameter (β_i) representing its scaled quality (beauty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bradley–Terry iteratively updates probabilities that item i beats item j; the resulting β parameters produce a scaled rank order of stimuli used for subsequent analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (IRR) via subgroup-split correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate reliability of CJ-derived scores by randomly splitting a demographic group into subgroups, deriving scores from each, and computing Pearson correlations between subgroup score-sets; repeat many times to get average IRR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper randomly split groups into subgroups of 12, repeated the process 1000 times, and reported average Pearson r as IRR. IRR values around .64–.72 were interpreted as indicating considerable agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize simplicity quantitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure simplicity of equations (as a predictor of beauty) by counting the number of characters in an equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting rules used: ignore commas; count mathematical elements and symbols as characters (e.g. dx/dt counts as 5); recognized as a crude measure but informative when testing the simplicity–beauty hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalize social influence quantitatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure potential social influence on perceived beauty by counting the number of mathematicians’ names mentioned in an equation’s description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a crude proxy for social influence/renown; results in the paper found number of names did not predict beauty scores, but source-label manipulations in prior studies did show social-conformity effects for some subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for description length
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure description verbosity by counting number of words in the accompanying description and include as a predictor/control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting rules: ignore punctuation and brackets; any mathematical element within description counted as one word. In this study number of words did not predict beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate materials into participants’ native languages for cross-cultural work
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting cross-cultural comparisons, present stimuli and instructions in participants’ native language rather than only in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses methodological criticisms of earlier cross-cultural studies and reduces artefacts due to language comprehension differences (c.f. Machery et al. 2017). The paper translated descriptions for Chinese participants into simplified Chinese.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful stimuli selection and balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Select stimuli to cover the domain of interest (e.g., equations drawn from existing lists, proofs from canonical collections) and consider constraints such as readability and participant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: selected 20 equations by taking every third from Zeki et al.’s 60-equation list; used fewer proofs (8) because proofs take longer to read. Include some famous items to probe mere-exposure effects but note familiarity should be measured if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure familiarity and understanding as covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: Include measures of participant familiarity with stimuli and self-rated understanding of stimuli, since understanding correlates with perceived beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior and related studies show positive correlation between understanding/familiarity and beauty ratings; without measuring familiarity one cannot test mere-exposure explanations for consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use linear regression and correlational analysis to test predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Predict CJ-derived beauty scores from stimulus features (e.g., character count, description length, number of names) using linear regression; report p-values and effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example results: number of characters significantly predicted beauty for British mathematicians and undergraduates (p=.008 and p=.010), but not significantly for Chinese mathematicians (p=.087). Report confidence intervals for correlations (e.g., r = .846, 95% CI [.645, .937]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare stimulus types (equations vs proofs) to assess generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether level of aesthetic consensus depends on the type of mathematical object by running parallel studies with different stimuli (equations, proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 1 used equations; Study 2 used proofs. IRR for proofs was slightly lower (r = .643) but still showed considerable agreement, suggesting consensus is not strictly a function of stimulus simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for method-induced artefacts (absolute vs relative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that methodological choices (absolute scales vs comparative methods, simultaneous vs sequential presentation) can produce differing conclusions about agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues comparative judgement may reveal consensus that absolute ratings miss; prior literature differences may stem from methodology rather than substantive disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use psychophysical justification for measurement choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground the choice of comparative judgement in psychophysics literature showing better human performance on relative judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Thurstone, Laming, Pollack, and other psychophysics work to justify CJ for measuring fuzzy aesthetic constructs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and test for social-conformity and mere-exposure effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Design manipulations or covariates to detect whether positive aesthetic evaluations are driven by exposure or source cues (e.g., revealing that a proof came from 'The Book').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work (Inglis & Aberdein 2020) manipulated source information and found source effects among pure mathematicians; include source manipulations when testing social influence hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor-analytic dimensions of proof appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize multiple latent dimensions on which proofs vary, as identified via exploratory factor analysis: aesthetics, intricacy, precision, and utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dimensions indicate beauty may not correlate strongly with simplicity or other single attributes; multi-dimensional appraisal of proofs is recommended when analysing proof aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed counting/operational rules for stimulus feature measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify exact rules for how features are counted (e.g., characters in equations, words in descriptions) so measures are reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example rules from the paper: for equations count individual characters ignoring commas; for descriptions count words ignoring punctuation and brackets; treat mathematical elements in descriptions as single words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and data-privacy assurances in participant recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain ethical approval, inform participants, and avoid collecting personal data when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study assured participants it had ethical approval and that no personal data would be collected; mathematician participants were asked only about AMS classification, career stage, and years worked (i.e., non-identifying professional info).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation of methods and refinement of operationalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple methods (e.g., compare absolute and relative judgements) and develop more sophisticated operationalizations (for simplicity, understanding) to build a fuller picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend future work directly comparing absolute vs relative approaches and improving operationalizations of simplicity and understanding to reconcile conflicting empirical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation details for CJ experimental protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical procedural features: recruit participants via department mailing lists; provide clear instructions; present randomly generated pairs; set a target number of judgements per participant; allow no time limit; use an online CJ platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example implementation: used No More Marking platform; participants completed 20 random pairwise judgements for equations; British mathematicians and Chinese mathematicians each had 24 participants completing 480 judgements; undergraduates had 81 participants completing 1620 judgements.
